title: Merge Intervals
description:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

Two intervals `[a, b]` and `[c, d]` are considered overlapping if they share at least one point (i.e., `max(a, c) <= min(b, d)`). In particular, intervals touching at a single endpoint such as `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` must be merged into `[1, 5]`.
hints: If you sort the intervals by their start value in ascending order, any set of overlapping intervals becomes contiguous in the sorted order.
Maintain the last merged interval in your result list. For each next interval [s, e], if s <= last_end, extend last_end = max(last_end, e).
Otherwise, the new interval is disjoint from all previous ones, so append [s, e] to the result.

examples.explanation: Since intervals [1, 3] and [2, 6] overlap, merge them into [1, 6]. [8, 10] and [15, 18] remain separate.
Intervals [1, 4] and [4, 5] touch at endpoint 4 and are considered overlapping, merging into [1, 5].
Sorting first brings [1, 4] before [2, 3]; since [2, 3] lies completely inside [1, 4], the merged result is [[1, 4]].
